title: Start with these five core skills
intro: Give these skills your first study session and most of your repeated practice. First make the JavaScript behavior clear. Then add TypeScript where it describes a useful contract. Study the broader lecture topics after you can build and explain the core flow independently.

skills.title: Read and write arrow functions
skills.why: An arrow function is a value that can be passed to another function or component. Its parameter receives an argument later. An expression body returns a value automatically; a block needs return when a value is required.
skills.evidence: Write both arrow forms from memory, return an object correctly, and explain the input and return value.

skills.title: Turn an array into visible components with map
skills.why: map calls the callback once per item and collects its returned values. A missing return produces undefined entries. Store the returned element array in a variable or place the expression inside JSX braces. Give each rendered sibling a stable key.
skills.evidence: Render a small list in both arrow styles, explain item versus items, and fix a missing return without guessing.

skills.title: Construct a new array for a state update
skills.why: Square brackets make an array, and ...previous copies its entries into that new array. A setter accepts either the next value or a pure function that returns it. For an append, setMenu(previous => [...previous, item]) is valid and uses the previous queued state.
skills.evidence: Append without push, show both valid setter forms, and distinguish array spread from object spread and a function block.

skills.title: Pass a parent callback to a child
skills.why: Put shared state in the parent. Pass the parent's update function as a prop. The child calls it in an event handler with the required argument. The parent updates state and the next render sends the new values down again.
skills.evidence: Build the parent and child from a blank file. Explain press -> child handler -> parent callback -> setter -> new render. Then adapt the string argument to a { name, popular } object.

skills.title: Use inference first and add types deliberately
skills.why: useState(initialMenu) can infer MenuItem[] when initialMenu already has that type. Empty arrays and null initial values often need explicit type arguments. Callback props need a clear function contract. TypeScript checks your code; it does not change the JavaScript callback behavior.
skills.evidence: Explain why one state call can infer its type while useState<MenuItem[]>([]) and useState<MenuItem | null>(null) need guidance.

callback_roles.returns: A transformed value, often a React element

callback_roles.receives: Event arguments supplied by the component, which you may ignore
callback_roles.returns: Its return value is not used as new state

callback_roles.receives: The argument the child passes, according to the prop type
callback_roles.returns: Usually void for an action callback

readiness: Before moving to breadth, complete exercises e01, e02, e04, e07, and e08 without opening their solutions. Then attempt mock m01. If you need a hint, record the exact step, repeat it later with different data, and explain the repair aloud. This is study evidence, not a guarantee about an assessment.
